topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Numbers on a number line
topic.description: Represent whole numbers as lengths on a number line and represent sums and differences within 100 on a number line diagram
evidence: Place whole numbers on a number line with equally spaced points
Show an addition as a jump forward on the number line (e.g. 38 + 27 shown as jumps)
Show a subtraction as a jump backward on the number line
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} mark numbers on a number line and show what happens when they add or subtract — for example, jumping forward 35 places from 48?

pedagogy.summary: Representing sums and differences on a number line is about mapping calculation onto MAGNITUDE: numbers are positions/lengths, and an addition is a forward jump of the added amount while a subtraction is a backward jump. The representational demands are that intervals (not tick marks) carry the quantity, spacing is proportional, and a jump's LENGTH is the amount added or subtracted (not its endpoint). Partitioning the jump (38 + 27 as +20 then +7) links the model to place-value strategy. The empty number line is the target tool.
bestPractices: Emphasise intervals over points: the amount is the SPACE jumped, not the marks counted — the classic off-by-one trap
Insist on proportional spacing so distance represents magnitude (a jump of 20 looks far longer than a jump of 7)
Model addition as forward jumps and subtraction as backward jumps, labelling each jump with its size
Partition jumps to mirror the mental strategy (bridge to the next ten, then the rest)
Move from pre-marked lines to the empty number line, and have children both READ a given diagram and DRAW their own
keyRepresentations: Empty number line (jumps labelled with amounts)
Pre-marked number line (equally spaced points)
Bead string / ruler (length model of number)
Partitioned jump (+20 then +7)
Backward-arrow subtraction diagram
commonMisconceptions: Counting tick marks (points) instead of intervals/jumps — off-by-one errors
Unequal or non-proportional spacing so distance doesn't represent magnitude
Reading a jump as its endpoint rather than as the amount added/subtracted
Drawing subtraction as a forward jump, or starting an addition jump from 0 rather than from the first number

learn.summary: Help 7-8 year-olds represent sums and differences within 100 on a number line by mapping calculation onto MAGNITUDE: numbers are positions/lengths, a jump's LENGTH is the amount added or subtracted (not its endpoint), addition is a forward jump and subtraction a backward jump. The key representational demands are that intervals (not tick marks) carry the quantity, spacing is proportional, and jumps can be partitioned to mirror place-value strategy (38 + 27 as +20 then +7). The target tool is the empty number line, and children should both READ a given diagram and DRAW their own.

activities.title: Build the jump: make each arrow's length equal the amount
feedback: If a jump of 20 is drawn the same length as a jump of 7, compare the two side by side against a ruler or scaled line so magnitude maps to length.
If the arrow is read as its endpoint ('+20' read as '58'), ask: does this arrow show the number 58, or does it show 'add 20'? What is the difference?
If subtraction is drawn going right, re-establish that subtraction moves left (gets smaller) and that a jump STARTS from the current number.
If the first addition jump is anchored at 0 instead of at 38, point out that the jump starts from the number you already have.
activities.rationale: A number line is a spatial-magnitude representation; letting a child size and place jumps so that length equals amount is intended to address the count-the-marks and equal-jumps errors as the child acts. An interactive version where arrow length is proportional (a +20 is longer than a +7) and that distinguishes forward-add from backward-subtract may make the mechanism concrete; this is an optional way to deliver the task, not the only way. Optionally, preserve the learner’s attempted arrow, compare it with the scaled target, then animate a corrected proportional jump and explain why its length changed; this feedback is a proposed scaffold, not evidence of superior effectiveness.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils represent and use number lines among the representations for numbers, sums and differences; number lines support addition as forward and subtraction as backward movement.

Children commonly misread number lines by counting tick marks rather than intervals and by ignoring proportional spacing; the empty number line is an effective model for representing addition and subtraction as jumps.
learnerActions: Start at 38 on a number line and add a forward jump of 20, then a forward jump of 7, landing on 58 then 65 (showing 38 + 27 = 65).
Notice and state that the +20 jump is drawn visibly longer than the +7 jump because the LENGTH of the jump is the amount.
Build 52 − 24 yourself using backward (leftward) jumps, e.g. −20 then −4, or −22 then −2 bridging 30, landing on 28.
Label each jump with its size and label the start and end points.
Both interpret a diagram you are given and construct one for a new calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: Distance on the line equals the amount: a jump represents 'add/subtract this much', not the point it lands on. Addition moves forward and subtraction moves backward, and partitioning a jump mirrors the mental place-value strategy.

activities.title: Label the spaces, not the marks
feedback: If the first mark is counted as 'one' of the jump, re-run it counting the gaps between marks instead.
If endpoints come out one off, re-step the jump labelling each space as you cross it.
activities.rationale: Explicitly counting intervals rather than points targets a common number-line error: counting tick marks instead of gaps, which gives off-by-one answers. Pre-marked lines and physical stepping aim to make the intervals tangible before moving to the empty number line.
sourceClaims: Children commonly misread number lines by counting tick marks rather than intervals and by ignoring proportional spacing; the empty number line is an effective model for representing addition and subtraction as jumps.
learnerActions: On a pre-marked, equally spaced number line, label the SPACES (intervals) between the marks rather than the marks themselves.
Physically step out a jump, counting the gaps crossed, not the ticks touched.
Check an endpoint: for a jump of 20 from 38, confirm it lands on 58 and not one mark off.
activities.intendedInsight: The amount is the number of intervals jumped, not the number of tick marks counted — this is the classic off-by-one trap.

activities.title: Interpret a given diagram, then draw your own
feedback: Reading correctly but drawing flawed lines (unequal spacing, starting from 0, or confusing amount with endpoint) shows partial command — practise producing lines from a blank start.
If spacing in a drawing doesn't match magnitude, compare against a ruler or scaled line.
Note: a hand-drawn or illustrated line is evocative, not exact, so proportional spacing can only be checked roughly; use a ruler or scale to tighten it.
activities.rationale: Interpretation exposes whether the child reads jumps as amounts and knows forward = add; translation exposes production errors invisible in reading (unequal spacing, counting marks, wrong direction, starting from 0). Requiring both read and draw gives a fuller picture of understanding; recognition or matching alone does not elicit the independent proportional drawing.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils represent and use number lines among the representations for numbers, sums and differences; number lines support addition as forward and subtraction as backward movement.
learnerActions: Interpret: shown a number line starting at 38 with an arrow landing on 58 labelled '+20' and then an arrow landing on 65 labelled '+7', state what calculation it shows (38 + 27 = 65) and what each jump means.
Explain that 27 has been partitioned into 20 and 7, each a forward jump of that amount.
Translate: on a blank line, draw a number line to show 52 − 24, using backward jumps totalling 24, landing on 28, with start, end, and each jump labelled and spaced proportionally.
Match number-line diagrams to the equations they represent.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a diagram and faithfully producing one are different skills; full command means you can do both, reading jumps as amounts and drawing proportional, correctly-directed lines.

constraints: Place whole numbers on a number line with equally spaced points; show addition as a forward jump and subtraction as a backward jump (within 100).
Intervals, not tick marks, carry the quantity; spacing must be proportional so a jump of 20 looks far longer than a jump of 7.
A jump's length is the amount added or subtracted, not the point it lands on.
Move from pre-marked lines to the empty number line as the target tool; have children both read and draw.

Matching diagrams to equations and drawing on a marked line can check interpretation and rough production, but recognition/matching alone does not elicit the independent, proportional drawing that shows full command.
Hand-drawn or illustrated number lines are approximations; proportional spacing cannot be rigorously assessed from an evocative illustration without a scale or ruler.
If points-versus-intervals is shaky, reteach the underlying number-line representation before proceeding.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One source (empty number line / misconception research) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claims, including that the empty number line is an 'effective model', as indicative, not confirmed.

The original row asserted '3D adds nothing' and 'talk cannot exercise the drawing-and-reading of a spatial representation.' These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened/omitted: a number line is primarily a 1-D/2-D spatial task that benefits from drawing, while spoken explanation can still support reasoning about it.

The original row framed an interactive tool that auto-stretches jumps as the moment the line 'stops being decoration'; this is a design claim, not evidence of efficacy, and has been presented as an optional delivery, not a requirement.

Efficacy wording in the activity rationales was kept to intended/may form because no cited source establishes that these specific activities outperform alternatives, and no source speaks directly to the read-versus-draw distinction beyond the forward=add convention.

probeDeeper: The arrow goes from 38 to 58 — does it show the number '58', or does it show 'add 20'? What's the difference?
Why should a jump of 20 be drawn longer than a jump of 7 — what would be wrong with the picture if they were equal?
Which way do the arrows point for a subtraction, and why?
If I drew the +7 jump LONGER than the +20 jump, what would be wrong even if the numbers were right?
assess.correctAnswer: Interpretation: it shows 38 + 27 = 65, with 27 partitioned into 20 and 7, each arrow a forward jump of that amount (a jump = an addition of its length). Translation: a number line from 52 with backward jump(s) totalling 24 (e.g. −20 then −4, or −22 then −2 bridging 30) landing on 28, start and end labelled, jumps sized and labelled, points spaced proportionally.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts the tick marks (points) instead of the intervals — a jump of 20 read/drawn as passing 21 marks, landing one off
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child label the SPACES between marks, not the marks; physically step the jumps counting gaps. Reteach number-line representation if points-vs-intervals is shaky.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Off-by-one endpoints; the child counts the first mark as 'one' of the jump

errorPatterns.pattern: Non-proportional spacing — draws a jump of 20 the same length as a jump of 7 (or ticks at irregular intervals)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare their jumps against a ruler/scaled line so magnitude maps to length; contrast a +20 and a +7 side by side.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the drawn line, distance doesn't match magnitude; big and small jumps look alike

errorPatterns.pattern: Direction or anchor error — draws the subtraction as a forward jump, or starts the addition jump from 0 instead of from 38, or reads a jump as its endpoint (the +20 arrow read as '58')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish that subtraction moves left (gets smaller) and that a jump STARTS from the current number and its length is the amount, not where it lands.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Subtraction shown going right, the first jump anchored at 0, or the amount and the landing point confused

responseLevels.gap: Counts tick marks, spaces jumps unequally, or points them the wrong way; the diagram doesn't map to the calculation.
responseLevels.full: Reads jumps as the amounts added/subtracted (not endpoints), knows forward = add and backward = subtract, and draws a proportional, correctly-directed number line for a new calculation with jumps and endpoints labelled.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a given number-line calculation correctly but draws one with flaws (unequal spacing, starts from 0, or endpoint/amount confusion) — can read but not yet faithfully produce (or vice versa).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First, interpretation: show the child a number line starting at 38 with two arrows drawn — a jump landing on 58 labelled '+20', then a jump landing on 65 labelled '+7'. Ask: 'What calculation does this picture show, and what does each jump mean?' Then, translation: hand them a blank line and say 'Now draw a number line to show 52 − 24.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The interpret move exposes whether the child reads jumps as amounts (not endpoints) and knows forward = add. The translate move exposes production errors invisible in reading: unequal spacing, counting marks, wrong direction, or starting from 0. A child who can both read AND faithfully draw understands the representation; one who can read a given diagram but draws a flawed one has only partial command.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Positive and Negative Numbers
topic.description: Understand positive and negative numbers as describing quantities with opposite directions or values; use them in context such as temperature, floors in a building, and bank balances
evidence: Represent positive and negative numbers on a number line and explain what zero means in context
Add a positive or negative number to any integer using number line reasoning
Subtract a positive or negative number from any integer, understanding that subtracting a negative is equivalent to adding
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees temperatures like −3°C and +5°C on a weather forecast, can they figure out how much warmer one day is than the other — even when the answer crosses zero?

pedagogy.summary: Understanding positive and negative numbers as quantities with opposite DIRECTIONS about a meaningful zero, and operating on them using number-line reasoning. The number line (or thermometer / floors-in-a-building / bank balance) is the central representation: a number's sign is its direction from zero and its magnitude is its distance. Adding a positive moves right/up, adding a negative moves left/down, and subtracting a negative reverses that to move right — so 'subtracting a negative is the same as adding' is derived from direction, not memorised. The recurring difficulty is distinguishing the two meanings of the minus symbol: the sign OF a number versus the operation of subtraction.
bestPractices: Anchor every idea on a number line / thermometer where zero is a real reference (freezing point, ground floor, break-even), not 'nothing'
Keep magnitude (distance from zero) and sign (direction) as separate ideas - counter 'bigger digit = bigger number' for negatives
Use directed-journey language: adding a negative is a move in the negative direction; subtracting a negative reverses direction
Distinguish the operation minus from the negative sign explicitly (colour, gesture, or bracket: 4 + (-7))
Derive 'subtract a negative = add' on the line (removing a debt / turning to face the other way) rather than stating a rule
keyRepresentations: Horizontal number line spanning zero (arrows for direction and length)
Vertical thermometer / floors of a building / sea level
Bank balance and debt (money owed as negative)
Two-colour counters (zero pairs) for combining opposites
commonMisconceptions: Orders negatives by magnitude - thinks -7 > -3 because 7 > 3
Conflates the negative sign with the subtraction operation ('two minuses', reads 4 + (-7) as 4 - 7 or 4 + 7 arbitrarily)
Believes numbers 'stop' at zero, so cannot count or move through zero
Thinks subtracting always makes smaller and adding always makes bigger (fails for negatives)
Treats 'subtract a negative' as more negative rather than as reversing direction

learn.summary: Positive and negative numbers are quantities with opposite DIRECTIONS from a meaningful zero (freezing point, ground floor, break-even), where sign is direction and magnitude is distance. On a number line, adding a positive moves right/up, adding a negative moves left/down, and subtracting a negative reverses direction to move right/up — so 'subtracting a negative is the same as adding' is derived from the direction of travel, not memorised as a sign rule. The central difficulty is distinguishing the two meanings of the minus symbol: the sign OF a number versus the operation of subtraction. Learners should both READ arrows/journeys and PRODUCE their own for new signed calculations, including moves straight through zero.

activities.title: Operate a directed number line: fire and flip the arrow
feedback: If the 1 - (-3) arrow is drawn moving LEFT to -2 ('subtracting a negative makes it more negative'): model on the line and with debt — subtracting a negative reverses direction (removing a -3 is adding 3); walk the arrow flip physically.
If 4 + (-7) is drawn rightward or read as 4 - 7 or 4 + 7: separate 'negative seven' (a directed quantity) from 'subtract' (a move) using brackets, colour and gesture for the two roles.
If the arrow halts at zero: continue the thermometer/lift below zero and count aloud through it (2, 1, 0, -1, -2).
activities.rationale: An operable line where the learner chooses the calculation and watches direction (sign) and length (magnitude) makes the structure of the move the object of attention, rather than a sign rule applied by habit. NCETM advises examining the STRUCTURE of the calculation rather than teaching sign rules; standards frame p+q as a distance |q| from p in a direction set by the sign, and p-q as adding the additive inverse. The through-zero journey for 4 + (-7) (passing 2, 1, 0, -1, -2 on the way to -3) covers an interval across 0 (7 units from 4 to -3), which links to the Year 6 statutory wording on intervals across zero; the 1 - (-3) journey does not cross zero. This is a research-informed design proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Pupils 'understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative' and 'understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p - q = p + (-q)', representing these on a horizontal or vertical number line (7.NS.A.1b, 1c).

Hart (1981)/CSMS records that when subtracting a positive integer many students 'simply subtract the numerals and then attempt to determine the sign for the answer', and when subtracting a negative use the rule 'two negatives make a positive'; the misconception is rooted in prior experience that 'addition makes larger and subtraction makes smaller', which breaks down for negatives. NCETM advises examining the STRUCTURE of the calculation rather than teaching sign rules.
Year 6 pupils 'use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across 0' (Year 6 Number - number and place value, verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Enter 4 + (-7): start a marker at 4 and draw/trace an arrow 7 units LEFT, landing on -3 — state that the negative sign IS the leftward direction and the 7 is how far.
Enter 1 - (-3): show that the arrow subtraction would send LEFT instead FLIPS to point RIGHT, landing on 4; compare with adding 3 (1 + 3 = 4) and confirm you land in the same place.
Say in words why the arrow reversed: removing a -3 (e.g. clearing a debt of 3) is the same as adding 3.

Replay both journeys vertically on a thermometer/lift mode: for 4 + (-7), count aloud straight down through zero (4, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3); for 1 - (-3), count up from 1 (2, 3, 4) and notice that this journey stays above zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Signed addition and the direction-reversal of subtracting a negative become visible: 'two minuses make a plus' is a direction reversal you can see, not a spell to recall. Numbers do not stop at zero.

activities.title: Zero in context and the two minus signs
feedback: If zero is described as 'nothing': re-anchor on a real context where below-zero values exist (temperature, basement floors, debt).
If the two minus signs are conflated: name 'negative seven' (a directed quantity) separately from 'subtract' (a move), and re-read the calculation aloud with that distinction.
activities.rationale: A fixed reference display supports reading direction, zero-in-context and the sign/operation distinction. It is a reference scaffold: it does not animate a calculation the learner chooses, so it complements rather than replaces the operable line, and it does not by itself show the learner can produce a move.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across 0' (Year 6 Number - number and place value, verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: On a labelled reference line/thermometer, point to a value and state both its sign (direction from zero) and its distance from zero.
Switch contexts (temperature, floors of a building, bank balance) and say what zero means in each (freezing point, ground floor, break-even — not 'nothing').
For a written calculation like 4 + (-7), mark which minus is the negative SIGN of a number and which (if any) is the subtraction OPERATION; use brackets/colour to keep them apart.
activities.intendedInsight: Zero is a meaningful reference point, and the minus symbol carries two distinct meanings that must be read, not guessed.

activities.title: Place, order and interpret signed calculations
feedback: If -7 is placed to the RIGHT of -3 (ordering by magnitude, treating -7 as greater): use the thermometer/line — left of zero is less, and the further left the smaller; contrast -7 and -3 directly.
If the given arrow's calculation is misread: separate direction (sign) from length (magnitude) explicitly and re-read the endpoints.
activities.rationale: Placing, ordering and reading signed calculations target the 'bigger digit = bigger number' error directly and rehearse separating sign from magnitude. The interpret action reads an interval across zero, which the Year 6 statutory wording supports; the ordering focus rests on the separated-ideas teaching principle rather than on that claim. Include a deliberate magnitude-ordering contrast such as -7 versus -3.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across 0' (Year 6 Number - number and place value, verbatim statutory wording).
learnerActions: Place -7 and -3 on a number line and state which is smaller, explaining via position (the further left, the smaller).
Order a set of negatives from least to greatest.

Interpret a given arrow (e.g. starting at -3, ending at 2): state the calculation it shows (-3 + 5 = 2, or the difference 2 - (-3) = 5, an interval across 0) and what its direction and length tell you.
Decide and justify which way 1 - (-3) moves before drawing it.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering by position (not by digit size) and reading an arrow's direction and length consolidate that magnitude and sign are separate ideas.

activities.title: Talk through the two meanings of minus
feedback: If the learner says subtracting always sends you left: revisit 1 - (-3) on the line and the debt model to show the reversal.
If the two minuses are described as the same thing: re-draw the calculation distinguishing the directed quantity from the move.
activities.rationale: A probing discussion can surface the two-meanings-of-minus confusion and whether the learner reasons about direction or guesses; it works best alongside the line, where the directional insight is seen, rather than in place of it. Discussion can elicit explanation but does not itself show the learner can construct an arrow for a new calculation.
sourceClaims: Hart (1981)/CSMS records that when subtracting a positive integer many students 'simply subtract the numerals and then attempt to determine the sign for the answer', and when subtracting a negative use the rule 'two negatives make a positive'; the misconception is rooted in prior experience that 'addition makes larger and subtraction makes smaller', which breaks down for negatives. NCETM advises examining the STRUCTURE of the calculation rather than teaching sign rules.
learnerActions: Answer: what is the difference between the minus in 'negative three' and the minus in 'subtract three'?
Explain which way your arrow for 4 + (-7) went and why.
Answer: does subtracting always send you left? What did 1 - (-3) do, and why?
Explain, using the line, which is bigger, -7 or -3.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the two roles of the minus symbol and justifying arrow direction surfaces and tests understanding beyond a correct final answer.

constraints: Anchor every idea on a number line/thermometer/floors/balance where zero is a real reference (freezing point, ground floor, break-even), not 'nothing'.
Keep magnitude (distance from zero) and sign (direction) as separate ideas; counter 'bigger digit = bigger number' for negatives.
Use directed-journey language: adding a negative moves in the negative direction; subtracting a negative reverses direction (right/up on the chosen axis).
Explicitly distinguish the subtraction operation from the negative sign using colour, gesture, or brackets, e.g. 4 + (-7).
Derive 'subtract a negative = add' on the line (removing a debt / turning to face the other way) rather than stating it as a rule.
A fixed reference poster/line supports reading sign, magnitude and zero-in-context but does not animate a learner-chosen operation; use it to complement, not replace, learner production of arrows.

Recognition/placement tasks (ordering, selecting a direction) do not by themselves show the learner can PRODUCE an arrow for a new signed calculation; include tasks where the learner constructs the move themselves.
Two-colour counters (zero pairs) are a useful alternative representation for combining opposites and may be offered alongside the line.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and legacy 'verified'/'confidence' flags are not independently confirmed. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a genuine third spatial dimension as adding nothing over a 2D vertical thermometer/lift. This is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; it is framed here only as a scope note (directed number is one-dimensional, so a vertical 2D thermometer/lift already represents that single directed axis) rather than a universal 'adds nothing' claim.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 4 + (-7) = -3 (7 left of 4); 1 - (-3) = 4 (reverse to move 3 right from 1, matching 1 + 3); -3 + 5 = 2 and 2 - (-3) = 5 — all consistent across the source fields and retained as stated.
The debt analogy ('removing a -3 is the same as adding 3') is a model of direction reversal, not a proof; present it as an illustration alongside the line.

Activity 3's single source claim directly supports its interval-across-zero interpret action; the ordering/magnitude focus rests on the separated-ideas teaching principle rather than on that statutory wording. The Year 6 claim on activity 1 supports the through-zero counting action, not the sign/magnitude-separation principle.

probeDeeper: What is the difference between the minus in 'negative three' and the minus in 'subtract three'?
Your arrow for 4 + (-7) went which way, and why that way?
Does subtracting always send you left? What did 1 - (-3) do - and why?
On the line, which is bigger, -7 or -3, and how does the line show it?
assess.correctAnswer: Interpret: the arrow shows -3 + 5 = 2 (it points right/positive, so something is added; its length 5 is the amount, matching the distance from -3 to 2) - equivalently the difference 2 - (-3) = 5. Translate: 4 + (-7) starts at 4 and moves 7 LEFT to -3; 1 - (-3) reverses direction to move 3 RIGHT (subtracting a negative), landing on 4. Distinguishes the negative sign (direction/position) from the subtraction operation (a move).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Subtracting a negative just makes it more negative' - draws 1 - (-3) moving LEFT, landing on -2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model on the line/with debt: subtracting a negative reverses the direction (removing a -3 is the same as adding 3); walk the arrow flip physically.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The translate step: the 1 - (-3) arrow points the wrong way

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates the negative sign with the subtraction operation - reads 4 + (-7) as 4 - 7 done arbitrarily, or as 4 + 7, unsure which minus is which
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explicitly separate 'negative seven' (a directed quantity) from 'subtract' (a move); use brackets, colour, and gesture for the two roles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Misreads the calculation the given arrow shows, or draws 4 + (-7) rightward

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude, so places -7 to the RIGHT of -3 on the line
errorPatterns.nextMove: Thermometer / left-of-zero-is-less; the further left, the smaller; contrast -7 and -3 directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endpoints placed wrongly; -7 treated as greater than -3

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes numbers 'stop' at zero, so an arrow crossing zero confuses or is halted there
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a thermometer/lift that continues below zero; count aloud through zero (2, 1, 0, -1, -2).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Arrow stops at 0, or the child cannot continue a move through zero

responseLevels.gap: Orders negatives by size, cannot cross zero, or draws arrows in the wrong direction; treats the two minus signs as the same thing.
responseLevels.full: Interprets and produces arrows for adding and subtracting both positive and negative numbers, articulates subtracting a negative as reversing direction (equivalent to adding), and transfers to a new case moving through zero.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a given arrow correctly and places integers on the line, but cannot reliably PRODUCE an arrow for adding a negative or subtracting a negative - knows the pieces but cannot translate a new signed calculation onto the line.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: First, INTERPRET: here is a number line with an arrow that starts at -3 and ends at 2. What calculation does this arrow show, and what do its direction and length tell you? Then, TRANSLATE: on the number line, draw an arrow to show 4 + (-7) and say where you land; then draw one for 1 - (-3) and say where you land.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reading the given arrow forces separating direction (sign) from length (magnitude). Producing an arrow for adding a negative (move left) versus subtracting a negative (move right) reveals whether the child understands subtracting-a-negative as a direction reversal or is guessing - and a child who conflates the operation minus with the negative sign draws 4 + (-7) or 1 - (-3) in the wrong direction. Interpreting then producing catches the child who can read a diagram but cannot build one for a new signed calculation.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Numbers on a number line
topic.description: Understand inequalities as statements comparing expressions, represent solutions on a number line, and solve simple linear inequalities using the same inverse-operation methods as equations
evidence: Write an inequality from a worded constraint (e.g., 'must be at least 12' → x ≥ 12)
Represent the solution set of an inequality on a number line with open or closed circles
Solve a one-step or two-step inequality such as 3x + 1 < 10

On a number line that range is shown by a circle at the boundary — open/hollow for strict < or > (boundary excluded), closed/filled for inclusive ≤ or ≥ (boundary included) — with an arrow or segment covering the values that satisfy it. bestPractices: Distinguish strict from inclusive explicitly: open circle = boundary NOT included (<, >), closed circle = boundary included (≤, ≥), tied to whether the boundary value itself satisfies the statement.
Represent the solution as a SET (arrow/segment), not a point; test a value inside and outside the range to confirm which side to shade.
Rehearse worded-constraint translation: 'at least 12' → x ≥ 12, 'at most'/'no more than' → ≤, 'more than' → strict >.

learn.summary: An inequality compares expressions and, unlike an equation, its solution is a RANGE (a set) of values rather than a single value. On a number line that range is shown by a circle at the boundary — open/hollow for strict < or > (boundary excluded), closed/filled for inclusive ≤ or ≥ (boundary included) — with an arrow or segment covering the values that satisfy it. Solving uses the same inverse operations as equations, except that multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign (an extension point). The core skill is translating fluently among a worded constraint, the inequality symbol and the number-line diagram, tying circle style to boundary inclusion, the arrow to the satisfying set, and rehearsing worded phrases such as 'at least' and 'at most'.

activities.title: Build and test a number-line inequality
feedback: If a value exactly on the boundary is marked as satisfying under > or <, ask: 'does the boundary value itself make the statement true?' For strict < or >, it does not, so the circle is open.
If the arrow covers values that fail the test, pick one value on each side (e.g. is −5 ≥ −2? is 0 ≥ −2?) to decide which side belongs to the solution.
If only the boundary point is marked, prompt that an inequality's solution is EVERY value in the range — mark several, then the whole arrow or segment; contrast with an equation's single answer.
activities.rationale: A live builder plus a 'does this value satisfy it?' tester makes boundary inclusion and solution-as-a-set directly observable, and letting the symbol switch recolour the boundary value ties the open/closed convention to a fact about solutions. Testing values on each side addresses reading direction backwards.
sourceClaims: Students have difficulty distinguishing > from ≥ and < from ≤ (whether the boundary is included) — shown graphically by whether a boundary line is dashed or solid, the coordinate-grid analogue of an open vs closed circle on a number line; they also shade/read the wrong side, and reason about the solution as isolated points rather than a whole region/set.
learnerActions: Choose an inequality symbol (<, ≤, >, ≥) and a boundary value, then draw the matching number line: decide whether the boundary circle is open or closed and which way the arrow points.
Test several sample values by asking of each, 'does this value satisfy the inequality?', and mark those that satisfy it (e.g. in one colour) and those that do not (another colour).

Switch the symbol from ≥ to > (or ≤ to <) on the same boundary and observe what changes: the boundary circle hollows, and a value sitting exactly on the boundary flips from satisfying to not satisfying.
Deliberately draw the arrow the wrong way, then test values along it to see that a whole stretch of the line fails the check — confirming direction matters.
Read a given diagram (e.g. a filled circle at −2 with a right-pointing arrow) back into symbols and words.
activities.intendedInsight: Inclusion is not an arbitrary drawing convention: whether the circle is filled depends on whether the boundary value itself is a solution. The arrow/segment represents the whole set of satisfying values, and its direction is fixed by what the symbol means.

activities.title: Translate worded constraints into symbols and diagrams
feedback: If 'at least 1' is rendered as x > 1 or an open circle, ask whether 1 itself is allowed — 'at least' includes the boundary, so x ≥ 1 with a closed circle.
If 'less than 4' is drawn with a closed circle at 4, check whether 4 satisfies 'less than 4' — it does not, so the circle is open.
Confirm the compound case by testing x = 1, x = 4 and a value between: 1 should satisfy, 4 should not, and the between-value should satisfy.
activities.rationale: Worded-constraint translation is the part of the representational skill most prone to slips between strict and inclusive phrasing; rehearsing the phrase→symbol mapping and checking the boundary against the words targets that error directly.
sourceClaims: Students have difficulty distinguishing > from ≥ and < from ≤ (whether the boundary is included) — shown graphically by whether a boundary line is dashed or solid, the coordinate-grid analogue of an open vs closed circle on a number line; they also shade/read the wrong side, and reason about the solution as isolated points rather than a whole region/set.
learnerActions: Translate worded constraints into inequality symbols: 'at least 12' → x ≥ 12, 'at most'/'no more than' → ≤, 'more than' → strict >, 'less than' → strict <.
Build a phrase→symbol reference table and, for each phrase, test the boundary value against the words ('is 12 allowed if you must be at least 12?').
Draw the number-line diagram for a compound statement such as 'x is at least 1 and less than 4' (closed circle at 1, open circle at 4, segment shaded between).
Check your diagram by reading it back into words and comparing with the original statement.
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday boundary phrases map precisely onto strict or inclusive symbols, and testing whether the boundary value is allowed decides between an open and closed circle.

activities.title: Solve a simple linear inequality and plot its solution set
feedback: If the solution is given as a single value, remind that solving an inequality yields a range — plot the whole arrow or segment, not a point.
If a test value inside the range fails the original inequality, recheck the inverse operations step by step.
For the negative-multiplier extension: test an actual value in both the original and transformed inequalities to see that the direction must flip for the solutions to agree.
activities.rationale: The curriculum requires solving linear inequalities and representing the solution set on a number line; tying the solved result back to the diagram reinforces that the solution is a set. The negative-multiplier rule is flagged as an extension rather than the KS3 focus.
sourceClaims: Pupils should 'solve linear inequalities in one variable ... ; represent the solution set on a number line' — this is the Key Stage 4 Algebra statutory statement (at KS3 pupils use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ and inequality notation a < x ≤ b).
learnerActions: Solve a one-step or two-step inequality such as 3x + 1 < 10 using the same inverse operations as an equation (subtract 1, then divide by 3, giving x < 3).
Represent the resulting solution set on a number line with the correct open or closed circle and arrow.
Check the solution by testing a value inside the range and a value outside it.
(Extension) Explore what happens when both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number, using test values to discover that the inequality direction reverses.
activities.intendedInsight: Solving an inequality mirrors solving an equation, but the answer is a set shown on the number line; special care is needed when multiplying or dividing by a negative because the direction reverses.

activities.title: Reference card: symbols, circles and directions
feedback: If a mapping is wrong (e.g. open circle paired with ≥), re-derive it from the question 'is the boundary value a solution?' rather than memorising.
Encourage pairing the card with an actual drawn example so the reference supports, rather than replaces, building the diagram.
activities.rationale: A static symbol-to-diagram reference supports recall but cannot by itself rehearse constructing or translating an inequality, so it is positioned as a check alongside the building activities.
learnerActions: Match each of <, ≤, >, ≥ to its circle style (open for strict, closed for inclusive) and, for inequalities written with the variable on the left (e.g. x < 3), to the direction of its arrow; notice that 3 > x means the same as x < 3, so the arrow still points left.
Use the card as a check when building or reading diagrams, confirming each choice against whether the boundary value is itself a solution.
activities.intendedInsight: The four symbols map systematically onto circle style; they map onto arrow direction once the inequality is written with the variable on the left (e.g. x ≥ a points right), giving a quick self-check reference.

constraints: A static reference card mapping symbols to circle style and arrow direction supports recall but does not rehearse building, translating or reading inequalities independently; pair it with construction tasks.

Matching, multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank items can check the representation (e.g. 'open or closed circle for x ≥ 3?', 'at least 12 → x __ 12') but recognition-style responses do not elicit independent construction of a diagram or translation; include tasks where the learner draws the number line and states the inequality themselves.
This content lives on a one-dimensional number line, so a three-dimensional representation carries no extra spatial payload for it; a 2D line with circle, arrow and test values is sufficient.
The negative-multiplier direction-reversal rule is a KS4 extension; keep the KS3 focus on the representation and translation.
Keep the solution-as-set idea explicit: an inequality's answer is every value in the range, contrasted with an equation's single value.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources support the existence of the boundary-inclusion/direction/set misconceptions and the curriculum requirement to represent solution sets on a number line; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity format, interaction, or medium.

The curriculum source labels the solve-and-represent statement as KS4 Algebra (KS3 covers the symbols/notation); activity 3 treats the full solving plus negative-multiplier reversal as an extension beyond the KS3 representation focus, consistent with the source.

Self-audit: the worked values (x ≥ −2 with closed circle and right arrow; compound 1 ≤ x < 4 with closed circle at 1, open at 4) are internally consistent, and 3x + 1 < 10 solves to x < 3 via one-/two-step inverse operations. pedagogy.summary: At 6-7 tool choice moves from purely concrete objects to REPRESENTATIONS — number line, hundred square, ruler, part-whole model — and the strategic act becomes matching the representation to the problem's PURPOSE and to the size of the numbers. A jump-counting addition suits a number line; a place-value addition suits a hundred square; a length problem needs a ruler. As numbers grow past ten, counting single cubes in ones becomes slow and error-prone, so a key lesson is trading the concrete tool for a representation that carries the tens. Press children to explain why one representation beats another for a given problem.
bestPractices: Sort problems by 'what are we trying to find?' and match the tool to that purpose (measure → ruler; jump-add → number line) before choosing numbers (EEF: clear rationale)
Show number lines explicitly — EEF finds them a particularly effective representation across KS2/3 — modelling jumps of ten rather than counting marks in ones
Compare two representations for the same problem and discuss 'which helped more and why', which EEF finds develops conceptual understanding
Make the inefficiency of counting big numbers in ones felt, so children choose a representation for efficiency, not just because it is allowed
Keep naming each tool's limitation (a number line doesn't measure a real object; cubes are unwieldy past twenty) so choice stays a fit judgement

Alternatives (a convince-a-partner dialogue, a primer comparison board) are intended to serve different pedagogical purposes.

activities.title: Pick the tool, work the problem, justify the fit
feedback: If the child builds 34+28 from single cubes and miscounts, or insists cubes are the way even for big numbers: contrast directly with a +20-then-+8 number-line jump, showing how the representation holds the tens so the ones needn't be counted. Revisit place-value adding strategies.

If the child grabs a number line for the measuring task: sort the two problems by 'what are we trying to find?' and match each tool's purpose; name what a ruler or metre stick does that a number line cannot here.

If the child reaches for a short ruler to measure the door: ask which measuring tool matches the size of the object, prompting the metre stick, so size as well as purpose drives the choice. Revisit measuring with length units.

If the child draws a number line but counts every mark in ones: model the +10 jump and ask 'can you get there in fewer jumps?', linking the tool to place-value structure rather than to the ritual of having drawn it.
Praise specifically when the child names both the efficiency gain (fewer jumps, no miscounting) and a case where the rejected tool would still win.
activities.rationale: A 2D surface with a tool palette lets the child actually pick, use, and feel the efficiency difference between a slow cube pile and a two-jump number line, then justify the choice. The same-child, two-problems contrast is intended to make the strategy concrete rather than a stated rule, though this specific activity is a research-informed proposal, not a separately validated intervention. Number lines modelling jumps of ten, and comparing two representations of the same idea, are highlighted in the EEF guidance.

learnerActions: Solve 34 + 28 using a palette of tools: cubes/base-ten, a number line, a hundred square, a ruler.
If you reach for single cubes, build and count 62 in ones — notice it is slow and easy to miscount. (Base-ten rods group the tens, so they avoid most of this counting.)
On the number line, jump 34 → +20 → 54 → +8 → 62 in two jumps.
On the hundred square (numbered with 1 at the top), add the 20 by moving two rows down to 54, then add 8 by moving forward eight squares (crossing into the next row) to reach 62.
After solving, answer: 'Why did that tool help?' and 'When would cubes actually be the better choice?'

Then tackle a measuring task: 'How long is the ribbon?' (a ruler fits, the number line does not) and 'How tall is the door?' (a metre stick fits better than a short ruler). Explain why the tool follows the problem's purpose AND the size of the object.
activities.intendedInsight: The right tool follows the PURPOSE of the problem and the size of the numbers or object, not habit: a representation that carries the tens (number line, hundred square) spares you counting ones, while a length problem needs a measuring tool matched to the object's size. Cubes remain a good fit for small numbers — this is a fit judgement, not a ranking of tools as 'babyish' or 'proper'.

activities.title: Convince a partner who defaults to cubes
feedback: If the child only says the number line is 'quicker' but cannot name when cubes would be better, prompt: 'Give me a problem where cubes really would be the BEST choice.'
If the child dismisses cubes outright as 'babyish', redirect to fit: cubes are fine, even best, for small numbers — the issue is efficiency with large numbers.
Affirm when the child both defends the efficient tool and identifies a genuine case for cubes.
activities.rationale: A dialogue partner who must be convinced can surface the fit-and-efficiency reasoning aloud and expose whether the child's reason is fit-based or status-based. This is intended as a complementary purpose to the hands-on palette: it targets articulation and justification rather than doing. It is a proposal, not a validated intervention.

learnerActions: Work with a partner (or in-role character) who always reaches for cubes, even for 34 + 28.

activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain why one representation beats another for a given problem — and when the rejected tool would in fact be right — is what separates a real fit judgement from a blanket ranking of tools.

activities.rationale: A static annotated comparison can prime awareness of each tool's purpose and lets the child compare representations, but on its own it does not let the child act, feel the inefficiency, or justify a choice; keep it as a brief primer before the hands-on activity.

constraints: Choose numbers large enough that counting in ones is genuinely inefficient (e.g. 34+28), so the efficiency case for a tens-carrying representation is real rather than asserted.

A single matching/recognition item can ask 'which tool?' but cannot observe the child using the tool or justifying fit and efficiency; recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of a strategy.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: counting backwards through zero into negative numbers, placing negatives on a number line, and reading them in context (temperature). The core insight is that the number line extends left past zero, and that −5 is LESS than −2 because it lies further from zero on the negative side — directly confronting the 'bigger digit = bigger' intuition. Work stays with counting, ordering, and reading in context; formal negative arithmetic is deferred. The primary vehicle is a number-line/thermometer activity the child drives, with reference images and conversational context as supports.

activities.title: Count down through zero on a thermometer line
feedback: If the child reverses upward at zero (0 then 1 again), extend the line/thermometer visibly below zero and re-count −1, −2, −3 so the continuation is seen; do not accept 'nothing is below zero'.
If the child says numbers stop at zero, anchor in a real below-zero context (temperature, floors below ground) so numbers less than zero are legitimate.
If the child reads −3 as 'three', pause and have them say 'negative three / three below zero' so the minus is read as a position/label below zero, not as a subtraction to carry out.
activities.rationale: Counting continuously down through zero lets the unbroken continuation past zero be experienced rather than merely stated, and the thermometer gives 'below zero' a concrete meaning. A horizontal line offers a second felt direction of decrease. A live, learner-driven scale (dragging the marker so the reading updates past zero) can make the continuation vivid, though a reference image or spoken counting can also support this.

The temperature/thermometer context and continuous counting through zero address the persistent −5>−2 ordering misconception.
learnerActions: Start at a reading (e.g. 3°C) on a vertical thermometer (or a horizontal number line) and count the marker down continuously: 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2, −3, watching it pass zero in one unbroken descent rather than stopping or bouncing.
Narrate each step aloud, including the names of the negatives as the marker crosses zero.
Repeat the descent on a horizontal number line, moving steadily left through zero, to feel that the decrease keeps going in the same direction past zero (toggle between the two if available).
Then count back UP through zero from a negative start (e.g. −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1) to check the sequence works both ways.
activities.intendedInsight: Below-zero numbers are a genuine continuation of the counting sequence, not a separate set; the line extends left/below zero, and counting down keeps going in the same direction past zero. Only the number names repeat as mirror images (1 and −1, 2 and −2), and each step down still gives a smaller number.

activities.title: Order negatives: colder is lower is smaller
feedback: If the child ranks −5 as larger because 5 > 2, walk both onto a horizontal number line: −5 sits further left, and further left means smaller, so −5 < −2 even though 5 > 2.
Reinforce with the thermometer image: a lower reading is colder, and colder is a smaller temperature.
If the child names 0 as the smallest possible number, use a below-zero context so numbers less than zero are accepted as comparable.
activities.rationale: The −5 vs −2 comparison is the central misconception, so it deserves dedicated ordering practice with an explanation, not just the correct label. Tying 'smaller' to position (further left / further below zero / colder) gives the child a stable rule that survives the digit-size clash. A drag-to-order interaction where −5 correctly lands below −2 with 'colder = lower = smaller' feedback can make the mechanism concrete; ordering on paper with stated reasons works too.
sourceClaims: The temperature/thermometer context and continuous counting through zero address the persistent −5>−2 ordering misconception.
learnerActions: Given numbers such as −5, −2, 0, 3, place each on the scale and arrange them smallest to largest.
Specifically compare −2 and −5: place both and decide which is smaller, stating a reason.
Explain in words why −5 is smaller than −2 even though 5 is bigger than 2 — e.g. 'it is further below zero / further left / colder'.
Answer context questions: Is −10°C warmer or colder than −2°C? Which is bigger, −1 or 0?
activities.intendedInsight: On the negative side, further from zero (further left / lower / colder) means SMALLER, so −5 < −2, reversing the digit-size intuition.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: drop below zero
feedback: A child expecting numbers to stop predicts 0 or 'it can't go lower'; show the continuation below zero and re-count through zero to −2.
A child who predicts −2 and justifies by continuing past zero (…1, 0, −1, −2) has the target understanding; ask them to explain the crossing point.
Follow-up probes: What comes after −3 if I keep counting back? If I started at −4 and counted up through zero, what would I say?
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task surfaces the 'numbers stop at zero' and magnitude-ordering misconceptions through the child's stated reason before the answer is revealed, making the diagnostic value come from the justification rather than the final label.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'count backwards through zero to include negative numbers'.
learnerActions: Set a thermometer to 3°C. Before moving anything, predict the reading after it drops 5 degrees, and say WHY.
Commit to the prediction and reason out loud (the reasoning is the important part).
Then slide/count the marker down 5 steps through zero to check against the prediction.
Discuss any mismatch: where did the count cross zero, and what came after?
activities.intendedInsight: Counting down past zero from 3 by 5 reaches −2 (3 − 5 = −2); numbers do not stop at zero, and predicting forces the child to apply the continuation rather than read it off.

activities.title: Negatives in the real world (context talk)
feedback: If the child treats −20 as warmer than −5 because 20 > 5, return to the thermometer: −20 is lower, so colder and smaller.
Keep the focus on ordering and reading; do not drift into adding/subtracting negatives.
activities.rationale: Context motivates and reinforces, and reading real sub-zero values gives extra ordering practice; the ordering rule itself is secured on the line, so context work supports and applies the idea rather than being the only route to it.
learnerActions: Discuss or read about places and situations with below-zero values: last night's temperatures, a polar region at −20°C vs −5°C, sea level, floors below ground.
Decide which of two sub-zero values is colder/lower and justify using the line idea.
Match a few real readings (e.g. fridge, freezer, a frosty morning) to positions on a thermometer scale.
activities.intendedInsight: Negative numbers describe real quantities below a chosen zero, giving the abstract line a meaningful anchor and extra ordering practice.

constraints: Keep to counting, ordering, and reading negatives in context; defer formal negative arithmetic (adding/subtracting integers) to later.

A static thermometer or number-line poster is a useful reference and can support counting, but cannot itself be dragged or stepped; pair it with active ordering/counting on a line rather than relying on it alone.
Conversation/context framing (e.g. a polar scientist) can motivate and give extra ordering practice, but should not be the sole route to the ordering concept.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Interpret negative numbers in real contexts (temperature, sea level, bank balance) and count forwards and backwards through zero with positive and negative whole numbers; place negatives on a number line and begin to find simple intervals (−4°C rises 7° → 3°C). Extends 'count back through zero' into using and reasoning with negatives.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): integers and their contexts are formalised in Grade 6 (6.NS.5-7); this is the pre-formal contextual foundation.
• Operational details — Ground negatives in multiple contexts (thermometer, sea level, money) and use the number line to count and to find intervals by 'counting the gap' through zero rather than by rules. Reinforce ordering (−4 < −1) and the meaning of the gap between a negative and a positive (the interval spans zero). Keep it count/interval based; defer formal signed arithmetic.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): places negatives on a line and reads a sub-zero temperature. Tier B (age 9-10, secure): counts through zero and finds a simple rise/fall interval across zero. Tier C (age 10, extending): reasons about intervals spanning zero in context and orders mixed positive/negative sets confidently.

activities.title: Count the gap through zero on a thermometer/number line
feedback: If the learner lands on 11, pause: starting at −4 is to the LEFT of (below) zero, so counting 7 steps right/up only reaches 3. Contrast with starting at +4, where 7 steps reach 11.

If the learner lands on 2, check whether they counted the starting value −4 as a jump or counted zero twice; if they land on 4, check whether they skipped zero (jumping straight from −1 to 1). Count the jumps aloud together: −4→−3→−2→−1→0 is exactly four jumps, then 0→1→2→3 is three more; reaching zero takes one jump of its own, so zero is counted once, never skipped and never repeated.
When counting backwards from 3, check that after 0 comes −1, then −2 — the count continues below zero rather than stopping at 0.
When the learner splits the count as '4 up to zero, then 3 more = 7 steps total, landing on 3', confirm they have read the interval positionally rather than by a rule.
For −4°C rising 7°, the interval is 7 degrees (4 up to zero, then 3 more) and the landing value is 3°C.
activities.rationale: Grounding negatives in multiple real contexts and finding cross-zero intervals by counting the gap on the number line (before formal signed arithmetic) makes the zero crossing concrete and directly targets the magnitude-ordering and double-counting errors; counting both forwards and backwards through zero matches the stated standard.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
Intervals across zero should be found by counting the gap on the number line through zero, in multiple contexts, before formal signed arithmetic.
learnerActions: Set a starting value in a real context, e.g. the temperature is −4°C, marked on a vertical thermometer or horizontal number line.
Apply a change, e.g. 'it rises by 7 degrees', and move a marker one step at a time, saying each value aloud: −4 → −3 → −2 → −1 → 0, then 1 → 2 → 3.
Deliberately split the count into two parts: how many steps up to reach zero (4), then how many steps beyond zero (3), and record the landing value (3°C).
Count backwards through zero as well: start at 3 and step down in ones — 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2 — saying what comes after 0, so you can move both forwards and backwards across zero.

Switch the SAME line into a different context — sea-level depth or a bank balance — keep the start and change equivalent, and notice the number behaves identically even though it means something different.
State in words where you crossed zero and why the total rise is 7 even though you land on 3.
activities.intendedInsight: An interval that spans zero is found by counting the gap along the line through zero — so many steps up to zero, then so many more beyond — not by a sign rule; you can count both forwards and backwards across zero, and negatives in different contexts behave the same positionally.

activities.title: Order and place mixed negatives and positives
feedback: If the learner places −4 as larger than (to the right of) −1, show both on the line: −4 sits further left/lower, so it is the smaller (colder) value; −7°C is colder than −3°C for the same reason.
Tie the feedback to the context: colder, lower, or more in debt all correspond to being further left on the line and therefore a smaller number.
Correct order smallest to largest: −4, −1, 0, 2, 5.
activities.rationale: Reinforcing ordering across zero with a concrete left-is-less experience confronts the seductive −4 > −1 magnitude error that the research flags as a common misconception.
sourceClaims: Year 5 pupils should 'interpret negative numbers in context, count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero'.
learnerActions: Arrange a mixed set such as −4, −1, 0, 2, 5 from smallest to largest on a number line.
Place a single value such as −3 at its correct spot on a labelled line.
Decide which of two values is colder/lower/more in debt, e.g. 'Which is colder, −7°C or −3°C?', and justify using position on the line.
Explain why −4 is smaller than −1 even though 4 is a bigger digit than 1, referencing left-is-less on the line.
activities.intendedInsight: On the number line, further left (colder / lower / deeper in debt) means smaller, so −4 < −1 < 0 < 2 < 5 — the size of the digit does not decide the order for negatives.

activities.title: Explain the context (optional spoken/role-play extension)
feedback: Prompt the learner to justify answers by referring to the number line or scale, not just a figure, especially when a change crosses zero.
If a change does not actually cross zero (e.g. −30 m rising to −18 m), confirm that too — not every rise or fall passes through zero.
Keep answers interval/count based; avoid introducing formal signed-arithmetic rules at this stage.
activities.rationale: A character or role-play can motivate multiple real contexts and generate interval questions; the interval reasoning itself is still best grounded on the number line, so this is offered as a contextual extension rather than the primary mechanism.
learnerActions: Take on a role such as a submarine pilot describing depths below sea level, or a weather presenter describing temperature changes.

Pose and answer questions like 'We were at −30 m and rose 12 m — where are we now?' (−18 m, still below the surface) and 'It was −3°C and rose 8° — how warm now?' (+5°C, passing up through zero), and explain the crossing of zero where it happens.
Reason aloud about which depth/temperature is higher or lower and how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Negatives describe real quantities (depth, temperature, balance); talking through changes rehearses counting through zero in meaningful situations, while noting that not every change actually crosses zero.

constraints: Use several contexts (temperature, sea level, money) so 'negative' is meaningful rather than abstract.
Find intervals by counting the gap through zero on the line, not by memorised sign rules; make the zero crossing explicit (e.g. −4 to 3 is 4 up to zero, then 3 more).
Support counting both forwards and backwards through zero, including stepping down below zero into the negatives.
Keep to counting and intervals in context; defer formal signed arithmetic to later years (US formalises integers in Grade 6; this is the pre-formal contextual foundation).

Ordering and placing tasks (ordering a set, placing on a line, fill-in-the-blank, multiple choice) can assess placement, ordering and simple cross-zero intervals, including the magnitude trap, but selection/recognition responses do not by themselves show the learner can count through zero and construct the reasoning aloud — pair them with the learner explaining their method.

A static thermometer or context poster is a useful reference and can introduce negative readings, but it cannot let the learner step through a changing value; use it as a scaffold alongside an activity where the learner actually counts the gap.
The 1D number line/scale is the natural representation for this topic; a 3D model is not needed here (this is a representation preference for this content, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing).
The role-play/spoken extension is optional and supplementary; do not treat it as a replacement for working on the number line.

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–12 — understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from zero on the number line; interpret it as magnitude in context; distinguish absolute-value comparisons from ordering statements.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): supports work on negatives and number-line reasoning; absolute value as magnitude underpins later work (bounds, error, modulus).
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.C.7c — 'understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from 0 on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation' and 7d distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order.
• Operational details: Define |x| as DISTANCE from zero (always ≥0), so |−5| = |5| = 5. Keep the distinction sharp between magnitude (how far) and order (which is greater): −7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|. Ground in context — a debt of −£30 is a bigger amount than −£5 even though it is 'less'. Read |·| aloud as 'distance from zero'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'What is |−8|?' Tier B: 'Which is greater: −9 or −2? Which has the greater absolute value?' Tier C: 'A balance of −£40 vs −£15 — which is the larger debt, and which is the smaller number? Explain.'

Paired statement cards contrasting order (<, >) with absolute value (|·|)

learn.summary: For learners aged 11–12: build absolute value as distance from zero on the number line (always ≥0, so |−5| = |5| = 5), interpret it as magnitude in real contexts (size of a debt, depth below sea level), and keep it sharply separate from ordering (−7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|). Read |x| aloud as 'the distance of x from zero', not 'make it positive'. A manipulable number line is the core activity; an annotated static line, a consolidation set of short items, and a context dialogue are supporting approaches with distinct purposes.

activities.title: Measure distance from zero on a draggable number line
feedback: If the learner expects |x| to carry a minus sign on the left of zero, point to the arc: it is a length, so it reads the same magnitude on both sides.
When the arc for −9 is longer than for −2, ask them to say aloud which number is greater (−2) and which is further from zero (−9) — two different answers.
At the crossing point, highlight that |x| touches 0 exactly at zero, then grows again in either direction.
activities.rationale: Absolute value is defined as distance from zero on the number line; making that distance visible and live as the point moves ties the symbol to its meaning and separates magnitude from order. The dragging/mirror/dual-read-out details are illustrative affordances, not required technology, and are a research-informed proposal rather than a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
KS3 number work develops reasoning with negative numbers and magnitude on the number line, underpinning absolute value / modulus.
learnerActions: Drag a point along a number line and watch a glowing arc from 0 to the point report its length as |x|, which is positive on either side of zero and is 0 only when the point is at zero.
Park the point at −5, then flip on a mirror toggle so the reflection at +5 lays down an identical arc — observe |−5| = |5| = 5.

Read a twin read-out that shows the signed value beside its absolute value; move the point to −9 then to −2 and notice the arc for −9 is LONGER even though −9 sits further LEFT (is the smaller number).
Drag the point across zero and watch the |x| read-out shrink to 0 and climb again — distance tracks how far from zero, never which side.
activities.intendedInsight: Absolute value is a distance (a length) from zero: it is never negative, two symmetric points share one absolute value, and 'further from zero' is a different question from 'greater number'.

activities.title: Annotated number line with distance arcs (static anchor)
feedback: If a learner reads the longer arc as 'the bigger number', separate the two questions: length of arc = magnitude; position left/right = order.
Confirm both arcs for −5 and 5 are the same length before moving on.
activities.rationale: A static annotated line anchors the distance meaning and the two-numbers-one-magnitude idea; it supports the same objective as the draggable version without live dragging and works on paper. It lacks the live across-zero movement, so add tracing tasks if used alone.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
learnerActions: On a number line, mark −5 and 5 and draw the arc from 0 to each, confirming both measure 5 units.
Reveal a callout that contrasts the order statement (−5 < 5) with the magnitude statement (|−5| = |5|).
For a second pair such as −9 and −2, draw both arcs and state separately which number is greater (−2) and which has the greater absolute value (−9).
activities.intendedInsight: Even without live movement, measuring arcs from zero establishes 'distance from zero' and the idea that two different numbers can share one absolute value.

activities.title: Consolidation: evaluate and discriminate
feedback: If a learner answers the same way to '−9 > −2' and '|−9| > |−2|', reread each using the number line: position for order, distance from zero for absolute value.
If an absolute value is given as negative, restate |x| as a length that cannot be negative.
activities.rationale: Evaluation and magnitude-vs-order discrimination are cleanly checkable in short structured items, making this a useful consolidator after the distance meaning is established. Recognition and selected-response items chiefly check and reinforce classification; they do not by themselves elicit independent reasoning or construction, which the number-line work is intended to develop.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
learnerActions: Evaluate absolute values, e.g. 'What is |−8|?' (= 8).
Match signed values to their absolute values.
Judge paired true/false statements such as '−9 > −2' (false) versus '|−9| > |−2|' (true), and explain each by the number line.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the distance meaning is built, learners can reliably compute absolute values and tell absolute-value comparisons apart from ordering comparisons.

activities.title: Context talk: larger debt vs larger number
feedback: If the learner equates 'bigger debt' with 'bigger number', place −40 and −15 on a line: −40 sits further left, so it is the smaller number though the larger debt.
Encourage the learner to state the two questions separately before answering.
activities.rationale: Grounding magnitude in debt/depth/temperature contexts targets the common conflation of magnitude with order and gives learners language for the distinction. Dialogue here addresses the contextual magnitude-vs-order question and works alongside the spatial number-line model; its advantage over other media is not established by the sources.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7c/7d: understand absolute value as distance from 0, interpret it as magnitude in context, and distinguish absolute-value comparisons from order statements.
learnerActions: Discuss a scenario: 'You owe £40, I owe £15 — whose debt is bigger, and whose balance is the greater number?'
Explain that −40 is the larger debt (greater magnitude) yet the smaller/lower balance (−40 < −15).
Try a second context (−8°C vs −3°C, or a diver at −8 m vs −3 m): name who is deeper/colder/further from zero and whose value is the greater number.
activities.intendedInsight: In real contexts, magnitude (how far from zero) and order (which value is greater) answer different questions, and conflating them produces errors like '−40 is the greater number'.

constraints: Define |x| strictly as distance from zero on the number line (always ≥0); avoid teaching it as 'remove the minus sign', which hides the meaning and fails for expressions like |x−3|.
Always pair order and magnitude explicitly (e.g. −7 < −3 but |−7| > |−3|) so learners do not assume greater absolute value means greater number.
Distinguish |−5| from −5: they are not interchangeable.
Recognition/matching/true-false items consolidate and check classification but do not elicit independent construction; use them after the number-line meaning is built, not as the primary teaching.
The static annotated line is a scaffold that lacks live movement across zero; if used alone, add tasks where learners trace the distance changing on both sides of zero.
A 3D representation was judged to add little because absolute value is a one-dimensional distance; this is a design judgement for this topic, not a general claim that 3D adds nothing to learning.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Place both on a number line: −3 sits to the right of −8, so −3 is greater. Reason from position, not digit size.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a context (−8°C vs −3°C): −8 is colder/lower yet 'further from zero'. Name the two different questions explicitly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Which is the greater number, −8 or −3? And which has the greater absolute value? How do you know?'

A child conflating them gives the same answer twice; a child who understands gives opposite answers and can justify each by the number line.
