topic.name: Square and cube numbers
topic.description: Use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube, and higher); recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, and 5; distinguish between exact representations of roots and their decimal approximations
evidence: Calculate squares, cubes, and higher integer powers of whole numbers
Find square roots and cube roots of perfect squares and perfect cubes
Recognise key powers (powers of 2 up to 2¹⁰, powers of 3 up to 3⁵, etc.) and distinguish exact roots from approximations
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out that √25 = 5 and ∛27 = 3 — knowing these are the inverse of squaring and cubing — and say whether √50 is closer to 7 or 8?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–14 — use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube and higher); recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, 5; distinguish exact root representations from decimal approximations.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube and higher), recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, 5' and 'distinguish between exact representations of roots and their decimal approximations.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 8.EE.A.1 (integer exponents) and 8.EE.A.2 (use square-root and cube-root symbols; √2 is irrational); 6.EE.A.1 write and evaluate expressions with whole-number exponents.
• Operational details: Define a power as repeated multiplication (base^exponent = base multiplied exponent-many times), tying square to area and cube to volume. Present roots as the INVERSE (√ of a perfect square, ∛ of a perfect cube). Distinguish EXACT surd form (√2) from a rounded decimal (≈1.414): the decimal is an approximation, √2 is the precise value. Recognise key power sequences (2¹–2¹⁰ etc.) for fluency. Respect BIDMAS for powers/roots in expressions.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'Evaluate 5³ and √49.' Tier B: 'Is √20 exact as a decimal? Explain.' Tier C: 'Which is larger, 3⁴ or 4³, and how do you know?'
bestPractices: Define powers as repeated multiplication with square→area and cube→volume made concrete before abstracting to notation
Present roots explicitly as the inverse of powers (√ undoes squaring, ∛ undoes cubing), including on perfect squares/cubes first
Draw the exact-vs-approximate line sharply: √2 is the precise value, 1.414 is a rounded approximation that never equals it
Build fluency with key power sequences (powers of 2, 3, 4, 5) as recognisable landmarks
Apply order-of-operations (BIDMAS) so powers and roots are evaluated in the right priority within expressions
keyRepresentations: Square array (area) for n² and cube stack (volume) for n³
Inverse-pair diagrams: 7 → (square) 49 → (root) 7
Power-sequence tables (2¹–2¹⁰, 3¹–3⁵) as landmarks
Number line contrasting the exact surd √2 with its decimal approximation region
commonMisconceptions: Reading n² as n×2 and n³ as n×3 (multiplying by the exponent instead of repeated multiplication)
Believing a rounded decimal equals the root (1.414 = √2) rather than approximating it
Assuming every number has a 'nice' exact root, or that √ always yields a whole number
Confusing square and cube (or their roots), especially in volume/area contexts
Mishandling powers in BIDMAS — evaluating left-to-right rather than powers before ×/÷

learn.summary: For ages 11–14: build powers as repeated multiplication (tying n² to area, n³ to volume), roots as the inverse operation, and the distinction between an exact surd (√2, √20) and its never-settling decimal approximation. Fluency with power sequences (powers of 2, 3, 4, 5) and correct order-of-operations handling of powers support the core conceptual work.

activities.title: Power/root workbench on arrays
feedback: If a cube comes out as base × exponent (e.g. 4³ = 12), rebuild it: 4³ is a 4×4×4 arrangement totalling 64 — count the repeated factors, not a single multiplication by the small number.
If a root is halved or divided (e.g. √49 = 24.5), reframe it as a question: '√49 asks what number times itself makes 49?' and test 7×7 = 49.

If √20 is written as a finished decimal, square your decimal (e.g. 4.47² = 19.9809; 4.472² = 19.998784, still short of 20) to see that these do not give exactly 20. Because 20 is not a perfect square, no terminating decimal squares to exactly 20, so the exact answer stays as √20.
activities.rationale: Manipulating square arrays makes power-as-repeated-multiplication and root-as-inverse concrete, and watching a non-perfect root's decimal refine without terminating makes the exact/approximate distinction visible. The live product, factor string, snapping of perfect squares, and persistent surd label are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube, higher), recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, 5, and distinguish exact root representations from decimal approximations.
learnerActions: Set a base and exponent: pick base 3, exponent 2, and watch a 3×3 square fill in reading area = 9; raise the exponent (e.g. to 4) and see a factor string assemble, 3×3×3×3 = 81 (that is 3⁴).
Switch to root mode: given an area of 49, resize a square until it fits exactly — side 7 — and record √49 = 7.
Given an area of 20, try to square off a whole-number side; observe that no whole side fits, the exact label √20 stays pinned, and a decimal read-out ticks 4.47…, 4.472… without ever landing.
State in your own words why √20 is the exact value while the decimal is only ever an approximation.
activities.intendedInsight: A power is repeated multiplication (not base × exponent); a root is the inverse that recovers the side/edge; and for non-perfect roots the surd is the exact value while the decimal only approximates it, never catching up.

activities.title: Build a cube to feel n³ as volume
feedback: If ∛64 is computed as 64 ÷ 3, rebuild the cube: three equal factors 4×4×4 = 64, so the edge is 4.
If a learner treats every root as exact, contrast ∛64 (exact, 4) with √2 (no terminating decimal).
activities.rationale: The cube case is genuinely spatial, so a physical or on-screen 3D build adds real meaning for volume and edge. This covers only the cube case: squares are modelled as 2D areas in the array work, and higher powers and the exact/approximate idea need the array and surd work above. Physical unit cubes are real objects with slight thickness used as models of the idealised geometric cube.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube, higher), recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, 5, and distinguish exact root representations from decimal approximations.
learnerActions: Stack unit cubes into an n×n×n cube (e.g. a 4×4×4 cube) and count the total to feel n³ as a volume.
Reverse the task: given a volume such as 64, find the edge length to establish ∛64 = 4.
Compare: say whether ∛64 is exact and how that differs from √2.
activities.intendedInsight: Cube numbers and cube roots have a genuine three-dimensional meaning (volume and edge), and perfect cubes give exact roots while numbers like 2 do not.

activities.title: Power-sequence reference wall
feedback: If a value is misread, re-expand its factor string to confirm, e.g. 2⁴ is four 2s multiplied = 16, not 2×4.
Point out that recognising 64 = 2⁶ = 4³ = 8² shows how the sequences overlap.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal reference supports fluency and recognition of the landmark sequences. It is a reference aid: on its own it does not elicit the repeated-multiplication action or the inverse root operation, which the manipulable activities provide.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils use integer powers and associated real roots (square, cube, higher), recognise powers of 2, 3, 4, 5, and distinguish exact root representations from decimal approximations.
learnerActions: Reveal values on a powers-of-2, 3, 4 and 5 wall, reading each value alongside its factor string (e.g. 2⁵ = 2×2×2×2×2 = 32, 5³ = 5×5×5 = 125).
Use the wall to recognise landmark powers (powers of 2 up to 2¹⁰, powers of 3 up to 3⁵, powers of 4 up to 4⁵ and powers of 5 up to 5⁴) on sight.
Spot which listed values are perfect squares or perfect cubes.
activities.intendedInsight: Key power sequences become recognisable landmarks that speed recall and help judge whether a root is likely to be exact.

activities.title: Consolidation: evaluate and classify
feedback: For 3 + 2², apply the power to its base first: 2² = 4, then 3 + 4 = 7 — not (3+2)² = 25.
For the exact/approximate item, √20 is the non-perfect one: its decimal never terminates, so it stays written as √20, while √25 = 5 and √9 = 3 are exact.
activities.rationale: Short evaluation and classification items consolidate fluency and surface whether the exact/approximate distinction and order-of-operations rule have taken hold. Recognition and fill-in items check fluency; they do not by themselves require independent construction of the concept, so they follow the manipulable work rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: 8.EE.A.1/A.2: work with integer exponents and use square-root and cube-root symbols; know √2 is irrational.
learnerActions: Fill in values: 5³ = ___ and √49 = ___.
Match bases to their power-sequence landmarks (e.g. 3 → 9, 27, 81).
Decide which of √25, √20, √9 is NOT exact, and explain why.
Evaluate a mixed expression such as 3 + 2² and explain the order used.
activities.intendedInsight: Once meaning is built, learners can evaluate powers and roots fluently, identify exact versus approximate roots, and apply order of operations correctly.

activities.title: Justify why √2 ≠ 1.414
feedback: If the learner insists 1.41 is exact, have them square it and compare to 2 — the gap (1.9881 ≠ 2) shows it is only an approximation.
Confirm that the exact value stays written as √2, just as √49 = 7 is exact because 49 is a perfect square.
activities.rationale: A guided justification discussion lets learners defend the exact/approximate distinction in their own words. Squaring candidate decimals gives an objective check rather than relying on assertion.
sourceClaims: 8.EE.A.1/A.2: work with integer exponents and use square-root and cube-root symbols; know √2 is irrational.
learnerActions: Discuss and answer: does 1.414 equal √2? Square 1.41 (= 1.9881) and 1.414 (= 1.999396) and report whether either hits 2.
Explain why no terminating decimal can equal √2, and what the exact value is.
activities.intendedInsight: √2 is irrational: its decimal never terminates or repeats, so any decimal is only an approximation and the exact value remains the surd √2.

constraints: Define powers as repeated multiplication with square→area and cube→volume made concrete before abstracting to notation.
Present roots explicitly as the inverse of powers (√ undoes squaring, ∛ undoes cubing), starting on perfect squares and perfect cubes.
Draw the exact-vs-approximate line sharply: √2 is the precise value; 1.414 is a rounded approximation that never equals it.
Apply BIDMAS so a power binds to its base before +, −, ×, ÷ (3 + 2² = 7, not 25).
The reference wall and the recognition/fill-in items are fluency aids and do not elicit the repeated-multiplication or inverse-root actions on their own.
The 3D cube build covers only the cube case; squares, higher powers and the exact/approximate idea need the array and surd activities.

Physical cube and card/array models have slight real thickness and are approximations of the idealised geometric figures; treat on-screen arrays as models of the number relationship, not as the figures themselves.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims are marked verified:false in the row; the cited standards support the stated teaching principles but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity or medium.

Self-audit arithmetic checks (all consistent with the source): 5³ = 125; √49 = 7; ∛64 = 4; 4³ = 64; 2⁵ = 32; 2⁶ = 64 = 4³ = 8²; 3 + 2² = 7; 1.41² = 1.9881; 1.414² = 1.999396; 4.47² = 19.9809 and 4.472² = 19.998784 (both just under 20), consistent with √20 ≈ 4.472 never landing exactly.
A trailing-ellipsis display of 4.472² in the first activity's feedback was corrected to the exact product 19.998784 to avoid misstating digits while keeping the 'never reaches 20' point.
The source's '3×3×3×3 = 81' is 3⁴ = 81; it is stated explicitly as 3⁴ here to avoid confusion with the 3² (area 9) example, since raising the exponent from 2 jumps to 4.

The original framing that a quiz is only a 'consolidator' and that non-manipulable formats 'cannot build' the concept has been narrowed to scoped affordance statements; catalog fit rankings were not treated as established pedagogical laws.
The reference-wall activity's source claim was corrected from the CCSS exponent/root-symbol claim to the DfE claim, which directly supports recognising powers of 2, 3, 4, 5.

probeDeeper: Why is 4³ = 64 and not 12 — what is actually being multiplied?
How are squaring and square-rooting related — how did finding √49 use that?
Is ∛64 exact or approximate? How is that different from √2?
What if I asked for √50 instead of √49 — what changes about the kind of answer you can give?

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Squaring means times 2, cubing means times 3' — computes 4² as 8 and 4³ as 12.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the geometric meaning: 4² is a 4×4 square (16 unit squares), 4³ a 4×4×4 cube (64); build one to break the 'times the little number' rule.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Powers come out as the base times the exponent rather than repeated multiplication.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats a root as division by 2 or 3 — gives √49 as 24.5.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe the root as a question — '√49 asks: what number times itself makes 49?' — and test 7×7; connect explicitly to the squaring just done.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Root answers are halves/thirds of the radicand rather than the inverse of a power.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats √2 (and other non-perfect roots) as exact terminating decimals — writes √2 = 1.41 with no sense it is rounded.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Square 1.41 (=1.9881 ≠ 2) and 1.414 (=1.999…) to show no decimal ever hits 2 exactly; establish that the exact value is the surd √2, the decimal is an approximation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States √2 = 1.41 (or 1.414) as the answer, no hedging, treats it like √49.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies the power after other operations — evaluates 3 + 2² as 5² = 25.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish order of operations: powers bind to their base before addition, so 3 + 2² = 3 + 4 = 7.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In a mixed expression the exponent is applied to a sum rather than to its base alone.

responseLevels.gap: Computes powers as base×exponent or roots as division; treats all roots as exact decimals.
responseLevels.full: Computes integer powers and perfect roots fluently, and distinguishes exact surd representations from their decimal approximations, justifying why a non-perfect root never terminates.
responseLevels.partial: Calculates perfect powers and roots correctly but cannot articulate why √2 is only approximable, or slips on order of operations in mixed expressions.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these on paper, showing what you do. (1) Calculate 4³. (2) Find √49 and ∛64. (3) Is √2 an exact number you can write down fully, or an approximation? Explain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch the working. A child with the power/root concept builds 4×4×4 and reverses squaring to root; a child running on a corrupted rule computes 4×3=12 for the cube or halves for the root. The √2 task is the sharp one: only a child who distinguishes exact surds from decimal approximations resists writing √2 = 1.41 as if it were exact.

topic.description: Appreciate the infinite nature of the sets of integers, real numbers, and rational numbers; position integers on a number line and distinguish between rational and irrational numbers
evidence: Explain that rational numbers can be written as a fraction of two integers and have terminating or repeating decimals
Give examples of irrational numbers and explain why their decimal expansions neither terminate nor repeat
Appreciate that between any two numbers there are infinitely many other numbers
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that numbers like √2 and π can't be written as exact fractions — and that their decimal expansions go on forever without repeating?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 13–14 — appreciate the infinite nature of the sets of integers, rational and real numbers; position numbers on a number line; distinguish rational from irrational numbers.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): develops the number system — rational numbers, the reals, and the distinction of irrationals (e.g. √2, π) — and the density/infinity of number sets.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 8.NS.A.1 (know numbers that are not rational are irrational; every rational has a terminating or repeating decimal, and conversely) and 8.NS.A.2 (approximate irrationals and locate them on a number line).
• Operational details: A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers and its decimal either TERMINATES or REPEATS; an irrational number's decimal neither terminates nor repeats (√2, π). Contrast the countable infinity of integers/rationals with the idea that between ANY two numbers lie infinitely many more (density). Locate irrationals approximately on the line via their decimal expansions. Distinguish 'infinite decimal' (can be rational, e.g. 0.333…) from 'irrational'.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 13): 'Is 0.75 rational? Give its fraction.' Tier B: 'Explain why √2 is irrational, not just "it has lots of decimals".' Tier C: 'Name a number between 0.12 and 0.13, then argue there are infinitely many.'
bestPractices: Define rational as expressible as a ratio of integers, tied to terminating OR repeating decimals; irrational as neither terminating nor repeating
Guard against 'infinite decimal = irrational' — 0.333… is infinite yet rational (1/3); the test is repetition, not length
Use density concretely: repeatedly find a number between two numbers to show infinitely many lie between any pair
Locate irrationals (√2 ≈ 1.414…, π ≈ 3.1415…) approximately on a number line while keeping their exact symbolic form
Give canonical irrational examples (√2, π, non-repeating constructed decimals) and canonical rationals (fractions, terminating/repeating decimals)
keyRepresentations: Zoomable number line demonstrating density (always another number between two)
Decimal-expansion classifier: terminating / repeating (rational) vs non-terminating-non-repeating (irrational)
Set nesting diagram: integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ reals, with irrationals filling the gaps
Fraction ↔ decimal conversions showing why some terminate and some repeat

Thinking √2 or π 'equal' their rounded decimals (1.414, 3.14)

learn.summary: For ages 13–14: build the distinction between rational and irrational numbers from the decimal signature (terminating OR repeating = rational; non-terminating AND non-repeating = irrational) and develop the idea of density — that infinitely many numbers lie between any two distinct numbers. The guidance aims to counter the 'infinite decimal = irrational' and 'discrete line' misconceptions, and to keep irrationals (√2, π) in their exact symbolic form while locating them approximately on a number line.

activities.title: Decimal-signature classifier: repetition, not length, decides
feedback: If a learner calls 0.333… irrational 'because it goes on forever', have them find and box the repeating 3 and write it as 1/3 — length is not the test; a repeat means rational.
If a learner calls √9 irrational 'because of the root sign', have them evaluate √9 = 3, a ratio of integers, and contrast with √2 whose value is not any such ratio; the symbol does not decide it.
If a learner treats 1.414 as 'equal to' √2, show the expansion continuing past those digits and keep the exact √2 pinned alongside the approximation.
activities.rationale: Classifying by decimal signature is intended to address the most common misconceptions (infinite-means-irrational, root-sign-means-irrational) and connects the fraction definition to its decimal behaviour. A streaming classifier that highlights a repeating block may make the repetition test concrete. If it reports 'no repeating block found', that only describes the digits shown, so irrationality must come from proof. This is an optional interaction example, not a required mechanism.

learnerActions: For each, write out or stream the decimal expansion and decide whether it TERMINATES or REPEATS. For √2 and π, note that a finite list of digits can never show that a decimal does NEITHER: some rationals have very long repeating blocks (1/97 repeats only after 96 digits). We know √2 and π are irrational because it has been proved, so their decimals never terminate or repeat.
Mark the repeating block when there is one (e.g. box the 3 in 0.3̅, or the 142857 in 1/7) and write the equivalent fraction.
State a rule in your own words for deciding rational vs irrational, then test it against √9 = 3 and 0.333…
Keep √2 and π written exactly as symbols, noting that 1.414… and 3.14… are only approximations.
Locate √2 and π approximately on a number line (e.g. √2 just past 1.4, between 1 and 2; π between 3 and 4) using their decimal approximations, while keeping the exact symbol pinned alongside.
activities.intendedInsight: A number is rational exactly when it can be written as a ratio of two integers — which shows up as a terminating OR repeating decimal. The deciding feature is whether the digits settle into a repeat, not how many digits there are: 0.333… is endless yet rational (=1/3). √2 is proved to be irrational, so its expansion never repeats. Checking a finite number of digits could never establish that on its own.

activities.title: Squeeze another number in: density of the line
feedback: If a learner says 'none' or a small finite count lie between two close fractions, walk through the averaging process twice. Then argue that averaging any two distinct numbers always gives a new number strictly between them, so the process never terminates and the count is infinite.
If a learner imports 'consecutive neighbours' from whole numbers, contrast finding the number after 5 (which is 6) with trying to find the number right after 0.12 — no such number exists.
Confirm when a learner articulates that the squeezing process has no end and therefore infinitely many numbers lie in any interval.
activities.rationale: Repeatedly constructing an in-between number makes density an action the learner performs rather than a fact to accept, and is intended to address the consecutive-number carryover. A zoomable number line that names a between-number then zooms to offer another is an optional interaction example that may make the 'well never runs dry' idea vivid; it is not the only way to teach density.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils develop the number system to include rationals, reals and the distinction of irrational numbers, and reason about the density/infinity of number sets.
learnerActions: Name two close numbers, e.g. 0.12 and 0.13 (or 1/4 and 1/3).
Find a number strictly between them — averaging the two is one reliable method (e.g. 0.125).
Now find a number between THAT one and the upper end, and again, and again.
Argue why this process can never run out, and conclude how many numbers lie between the original pair.
Explain why there is no 'next' number after a given one, unlike the integers.
activities.intendedInsight: Between any two distinct numbers there are infinitely many others, so the number line is dense: there is no smallest gap and no 'next' number. This contrasts with the discrete, consecutive structure of the integers.

activities.title: Dialogue: why √2 cannot be a fraction
feedback: If a learner justifies √2's irrationality only by 'it has lots of decimals', redirect to the structural argument that no integer ratio can equal it.
If a learner claims a number comes 'right after' 0.12, ask them to name it, then name one between 0.12 and their answer — surfacing density.
Acknowledge that the full proof-by-contradiction is challenging; partial reasoning that grasps 'no integer ratio works' is valuable progress.
activities.rationale: This philosophically rich topic (what infinity means, why √2 is not a fraction, whether there is a next number) suits Socratic dialogue that can probe and challenge intuitions. Dialogue is offered as a complementary approach to the manipulatives, each exposing different facets; it is not claimed to be superior to or necessary over hands-on classification.
learnerActions: Work through the classic argument: suppose √2 = a/b in lowest terms, and reason about whether a and b can both be chosen with no common factor.
Respond to Socratic prompts about what would have to be true of a² and b², and where a contradiction arises.
Then tackle the intuition probe: 'Is there a number right after 0.12?' and explain your answer.

Try to write π as a fraction of two whole numbers (e.g. 22/7 or 355/113) and check that these are only approximations. Note that mathematicians have proved π is irrational, though the proof is beyond this level, which is why its decimal never terminates or repeats.
activities.intendedInsight: Some numbers genuinely cannot be written as a ratio of integers — this is a provable fact, not just 'it has lots of decimals'. Engaging with the proof-by-contradiction and the 'no next number' question deepens understanding of what irrationality and density actually mean.

activities.title: Reference anchor: nested number sets
feedback: If a learner places √9 among the irrationals, have them evaluate it (=3) and move it into the integers/rationals.
If a learner cannot place 0.333…, have them recall its fraction (1/3) and place it with the rationals.
activities.rationale: A set-nesting diagram is a useful static reference that organises the vocabulary and relationships. Note its limit: a fixed diagram anchors structure but does not by itself demonstrate density or classify expansions dynamically, so pair it with the active tasks above.
learnerActions: Study a nested-sets diagram: integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ reals, with irrationals filling the gaps in the reals.
For each region, note example numbers and their decimal signature (terminating / repeating / non-repeating).
Place given numbers into the correct region and justify the placement by the rational/irrational test.
activities.intendedInsight: The number systems nest: every integer is rational, every rational is real, and irrationals occupy the reals that are not rational. This gives a map for where any number sits.

activities.title: Consolidation: sort and justify
feedback: Recognition sorting confirms classification but does not by itself show independent reasoning — require a stated justification for each item.
If a learner picks the wrong item, ask them to name the decimal signature that justifies each option before re-choosing.
activities.rationale: Sorting and selected-response items cleanly assess the decimal-signature distinction and make good consolidators AFTER the concept is constructed. Treat selected-response as a check that follows construction; requiring a justification keeps it from being pure recognition.

learnerActions: Sort a mixed set (e.g. 0.333…, √2, 3/8, 0.25, √9, π) into rational vs irrational.
Choose which of a list is irrational and explain the reason, not just the choice (e.g. 'which is irrational: 0.333…, √2, 3/8, 0.25?').
Given a repeating decimal, write the equivalent fraction.
For a classification you make, state the decision rule you applied.
activities.intendedInsight: Once the concepts are built, fluent classification and fraction-recovery confirm that the learner applies the repetition/ratio test rather than surface cues.

constraints: Keep irrationals in exact symbolic form (√2, π); treat 1.414… and 3.14… as approximations, never as equal to the exact value.
The decision test is repetition/terminability (equivalently, expressibility as a ratio of integers), NOT how long or 'messy' the decimal looks — 0.333… is rational.
The root symbol does not determine irrationality: √9 = 3 is rational while √2 is irrational; evaluate the value.
A static nested-sets diagram is a reference scaffold: it anchors vocabulary and structure but does not demonstrate density or dynamically classify expansions, so it should accompany active tasks.
Selected-response/sorting tasks are consolidators that follow concept-building; pair them with required justifications so they elicit reasoning rather than recognition alone.

Tier the challenge: age-13 checkpoint 'Is 0.75 rational? Give its fraction'; mid 'Explain why √2 is irrational, not just that it has lots of decimals'; stretch 'Name a number between 0.12 and 0.13, then argue there are infinitely many.'
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified, and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'conversation' entry's proof-by-contradiction for √2 is mathematically standard but demanding for ages 13–14; it is retained as an exploratory dialogue with the caveat that partial reasoning is acceptable, and is not asserted as more effective than the manipulative approaches.

The original claims that a dialogue can probe intuitions 'in ways a manipulative cannot' and that '3D adds nothing' were catalog fit-rankings; these have been softened or dropped — the 3D option was omitted as it carried no distinct learning action and risked implying spurious structure on a one-dimensional topic.

The pedagogy's contrast between the countable infinity of integers/rationals and the density of the reals is an advanced nuance; this rewrite develops density but does not separately treat countability — add it only if learners are ready.
The two reteach prerequisite IDs and one null in the source error patterns are internal references not reproduced in learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: What is the actual test for whether a decimal is rational — length, or something else?
Give me a number between 1/4 and 1/3 — now one between THAT and 1/3.
Is √16 rational or irrational? How do you decide?
Can you write π as a fraction of two whole numbers? Why does that matter here?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.333... is rational — it equals 1/3, a ratio of two integers, and a repeating decimal is always rational. There are infinitely many numbers between 1/4 and 1/3 (indeed between any two distinct numbers).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Non-terminating decimal = irrational' — calls 0.333... irrational because it never ends.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish repeating (rational: 0.333...=1/3, 0.142857...=1/7) from non-repeating-non-terminating (irrational: π, √2); the test is the pattern, not the length.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child cites 'goes on forever' as proof of irrationality, ignoring the repeat.

errorPatterns.pattern: Consecutive-number / discreteness carryover — thinks there are no (or only a few) numbers between 1/4 and 1/3, as if fractions have 'next' neighbours like integers.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find a number between (e.g. average them), then between that and 1/3, and again — show the process never stops, so infinitely many lie between; the line is dense.
errorPatterns.distractor: None — they're right next to each other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 'none', 'one', or a small finite count for numbers between the two fractions.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Irrational = anything with a root or a messy decimal' — calls √9 irrational, or thinks all surds are irrational.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Evaluate √9 = 3 (rational) versus √2 (irrational); the root symbol does not decide it — whether the value is a ratio of integers does.
errorPatterns.distractor: √9 is irrational because it's a root.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child labels √9 (=3) or a rounded decimal as irrational on sight of the root sign.

responseLevels.gap: Equates infinite/root with irrational; treats the line as discrete (finite numbers between fractions).
responseLevels.full: Classifies by whether a value is a ratio of integers (repeating/terminating = rational; non-repeating-non-terminating = irrational), gives correct examples, and explains that infinitely many numbers lie between any two distinct numbers.
responseLevels.partial: Can classify clear cases but relies on 'goes on forever' or the root sign as the test, or is unsure about density between fractions.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Is 0.333... (the 3 repeating forever) rational or irrational? And how many numbers are there between 1/4 and 1/3? Explain both.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the rational/irrational distinction knows 'goes on forever' is not the test — REPEATING or terminating means rational, only non-repeating-non-terminating is irrational — and grasps the density of the number line. A child equating 'infinite decimal' with 'irrational', or importing whole-number 'consecutive' thinking, answers differently and reveals the misconception in the reason.
